pairs.question: Why is quitting smoking so important?
pairs.answer: Tobacco use remains the leading preventable cause of disease, disability, and death in the United States. It's crucial to focus on quitting to improve health outcomes.
pairs.evidence: Tobacco use remains the leading preventable cause of disease, disability, and death in the United States, making tobacco and smoking prevention, cessation and policy issues a top public health priority.

pairs.question: Are smoking rates really going down?
pairs.answer: Yes, rates of cigarette use continue to drop, especially among adults. However, vaping and other forms of nicotine use are increasing, particularly among younger users.
pairs.evidence: Even as rates of cigarette use continue to drop, especially among adults, vaping and other forms of nicotine use—particularly in younger users—are increasing.

pairs.question: How often do tobacco users see their doctors?
pairs.answer: About 70% of people who use tobacco products see a physician each year. This gives you a great opportunity to discuss quitting.
pairs.evidence: About 70% of people who use tobacco products see a physician each year, so you can make an impact on your patients' tobacco use, including those with behavioral health disorders.

pairs.question: What impact can doctors have on smoking cessation?
pairs.answer: If family physicians advised 90% of smokers to quit and offered them medication or assistance, about 42,000 lives could be saved. Your advice really matters!
pairs.evidence: About 42,000 lives could be saved if family physicians would advise 90% of smokers to quit, and offer them medication or other assistance.

pairs.question: Do evidence-based interventions really help with quitting?
pairs.answer: Yes, tobacco cessation more than doubles when evidence-based interventions are used. Your efforts can make a significant difference.
pairs.evidence: Tobacco cessation more than doubles when evidence-based interventions are used. Your efforts make a difference.

pairs.question: Should I talk to my doctor about my tobacco use?
pairs.answer: Yes, clinicians are advised to ask all adults about tobacco use. It's important to discuss your habits so you can get the right support to quit.
pairs.evidence: Clinicians are advised to ask all adults about tobacco use, advise them to stop using tobacco and provide behavioral interventions and FDA-approved pharmacotherapy for cessation to nonpregnant adults who use tobacco.

pairs.question: What should I do if I'm pregnant and using tobacco?
pairs.answer: If you're pregnant and using tobacco, it's crucial to talk to your healthcare provider. They are advised to provide behavioral interventions to help you stop using tobacco.
pairs.evidence: Clinicians are advised to ask all pregnant persons about tobacco use, advise them to stop using tobacco and provide behavioral interventions for cessation to pregnant persons who use tobacco.

pairs.question: What can be done to prevent kids from starting to smoke?
pairs.answer: Primary care clinicians are encouraged to provide interventions to prevent tobacco use among school-aged children and adolescents. Education and brief counseling can be effective.
pairs.evidence: The AAFP supports the USPSTF clinical preventive service recommendation on this topic: that primary care clinicians provide interventions, including education or brief counseling, to prevent initiation of tobacco use among school-aged children and adolescents.

pairs.question: How does smoking affect my medications?
pairs.answer: Tobacco smoke can negatively impact the efficacy of certain medications. If you smoke or vape, you may require higher doses of some medications.
pairs.evidence: Tobacco smoke can negatively impact the efficacy of certain medications, so patients who smoke or vape may require higher doses.

pairs.question: What kind of support can I get to quit smoking?
pairs.answer: You can receive behavioral interventions and FDA-approved pharmacotherapy to help you quit. It's important to reach out for support.
pairs.evidence: Clinicians are advised to ask all adults about tobacco use, advise them to stop using tobacco and provide behavioral interventions and FDA-approved pharmacotherapy for cessation to nonpregnant adults who use tobacco.

pairs.question: Is there a specific approach for adolescents who smoke?
pairs.answer: Yes, interventions for adolescents include education and brief counseling to prevent tobacco use. It's essential to address this early.
pairs.evidence: The AAFP supports the USPSTF clinical preventive service recommendation on this topic: that primary care clinicians provide interventions, including education or brief counseling, to prevent initiation of tobacco use among school-aged children and adolescents.

pairs.question: Are there any resources to help me quit smoking?
pairs.answer: The Smoking Cessation Leadership Center at the University of California, San Francisco offers tailored support, including webinars, toolkits, and quit now cards. These resources can really help you on your journey to quit.
pairs.evidence: The Smoking Cessation Leadership Center at the University of California, San Francisco, offers tailored support with a focus on underserved populations (e.g., webinars, toolkits, articles and reports, fact sheets and guides, quit now cards).

pairs.question: What percentage of smokers wanted to quit last year?
pairs.answer: About 67.7% of adult smokers who were able to quit successfully in the past year said they wanted to quit. It's great to know that many people share this goal!
pairs.evidence: Adult smokers who were able to quit successfully in the past year; 67.7% said they wanted to quit and 53.3% said they had tried.

pairs.question: Can telehealth help me quit smoking?
pairs.answer: Yes, telehealth can be an effective supplement to in-person visits when helping a patient quit smoking or vaping. It allows for remote follow-ups that can make you feel more supported.
pairs.evidence: Telehealth can be an effective supplement to in-person visits when helping a patient quit smoking or vaping.

pairs.question: How can my doctor keep track of my smoking habits?
pairs.answer: The AAFP advocates for electronic health records (EHRs) that include templates to collect information about tobacco use, secondhand smoke exposure, and past quit attempts. This helps your doctor provide better care.
pairs.evidence: The AAFP advocates for EHRs that include a template prompting clinicians or their practice teams to collect information about tobacco and nicotine use, secondhand smoke exposure, cessation interest and past quit attempts.

pairs.question: Is there a way to get more support for quitting smoking?
pairs.answer: Absolutely! Following up remotely through telehealth can help you feel more supported while quitting. It also allows clinical staff to gauge non-verbal cues that might be missed during a phone call.
pairs.evidence: Following up remotely can make patients feel more supported. Telehealth allows clinical staff to gauge non-verbal cues that can be missed during a telephone appointment.

pairs.question: What kind of counseling is available for people like me who smoke?

pairs.question: Is there special support for pregnant women trying to quit smoking?

pairs.question: How can I make sure my doctor gets paid for helping me quit smoking?
pairs.answer: Accurate billing and coding is a must so you can be compensated for these services. Make sure to discuss this with your healthcare provider.
pairs.evidence: Accurate billing and coding is a must so you can be compensated for these services.
